full_name: Stochastic mirror descent for stochastic convex-concave saddle point problems
source_reference: Lan, First-order and Stochastic Optimization Methods for Machine Learning, Springer 2020, Section 4.3.1, Lemma 4.6, equations (4.3.8)-(4.3.17), and Proposition 4.10

problem.description: Stochastic convex-concave minimax problem with finite-valued expectation.

variable_space.description: Source prose states that X ⊂ Rn and Y ⊂ Rm are nonempty bounded closed convex sets; later it says: We use notation z = (x, y) and equip Z := X × Y with the distance generating function.

assumptions.name: Convex_concave_problem_data
assumptions.description: Here X ⊂ Rn and Y ⊂ Rm are nonempty bounded closed convex sets, ξ is a random vector whose probability distribution P is supported on set Ξ ⊂ Rd and Φ : X ×Y × Ξ → R.

assumptions.name: Finite_expectation_and_convexity_concavity
assumptions.description: We assume that for every ξ ∈ Ξ, function Φ(x,y,ξ) is convex in x ∈ X and concave in y ∈ Y, and for all x ∈ X, y ∈ Y the expectation is well defined and finite valued. It follows that φ(x,y) is convex in x ∈ X and concave in y ∈ Y, finite valued.

assumptions.name: Phi_lipschitz_continuity
assumptions.description: In addition, we assume that φ (·, ·) is Lipschitz continuous on X × Y.

assumptions.name: Stochastic_first_order_oracle_Assumption_7
assumptions.description: There exists a stochastic first-order oracle which for every given x ∈ X, y ∈ Y and ξ ∈ Ξ returns value Φ(x,y,ξ) and a stochastic subgradient; g(x,y) is well defined, and gx(x,y) ∈ ∂x φ(x,y) and −gy(x,y) ∈ ∂y(−φ(x,y)).

assumptions.name: Distance_generating_functions_modulus_one
assumptions.description: We equip X and Y with distance generating functions νX : X → R modulus 1 with respect to · X, and νY : Y → R modulus 1 with respect to · Y. Let DX ≡ DX,νX and DY ≡ DY,νY be the respective constants (see Sect. 3.2).

assumptions.name: Product_DGF_normalization
assumptions.description: The following prose states that ν is a distance generating function for Z modulus 1 with respect to the product norm, that Z^o = X^o × Y^o and D_Z ≡ D_{Z,ν} = 1, and that V(z,u) : Z^o × Z → R is the associated prox-function.

assumptions.name: Mirror_descent_update_3_2_5
assumptions.description: The deterministic mirror descent prox subproblem whose optimality condition is used in Lemma 3.4.

assumptions.name: Stochastic_mirror_descent_initialization_z1
assumptions.description: where the initial point z1 ∈ Z is chosen to be the minimizer of ν(z) on Z.

assumptions.name: Stochastic_mirror_descent_update_4_3_6
assumptions.description: The stochastic mirror descent recursion as printed in (4.3.6). The proof of Lemma 4.6 later applies (4.1.41) with \zeta_t=\gamma_tG(z_t,\xi_t), so the prox-recursion form needed for that application is recorded as a derived proof-side interpretation rather than as the printed formula.

assumptions.name: Error_measure_definition
assumptions.math: \varepsilon_\phi(\tilde z):=\left[\max_{y\in Y}\phi(\tilde x,y)-\phi_*\right]+\left[\phi_*-\min_{x\in X}\phi(x,\tilde y)\right]=\max_{y\in Y}\phi(\tilde x,y)-\min_{x\in X}\phi(x,\tilde y).

assumptions.name: Exponential_tail_oracle_bound
assumptions.description: Suppose that conditions of the bound (4.3.16) are verified and, further, it holds for all (u,v) ∈ Z that the two displayed exponential moment inequalities in (4.3.18) hold.

initialization.description: where the initial point z1 ∈ Z is chosen to be the minimizer of ν(z) on Z.

main_theorem.rate: O(\bar D_{Z,\nu} M / sqrt(j)) for the decreasing-stepsize sliding average, with \bar D_{Z,\nu} assumed finite as in the paper; O(M / sqrt(N)) for the fixed-horizon constant stepsize.

proof.description: Define the saddle-point error for an approximate solution and rewrite it as the max-min gap.
proof.math: \varepsilon_\phi(\tilde z):=\left[\max_{y\in Y}\phi(\tilde x,y)-\phi_*\right]+\left[\phi_*-\min_{x\in X}\phi(x,\tilde y)\right]=\max_{y\in Y}\phi(\tilde x,y)-\min_{x\in X}\phi(x,\tilde y).

proof.description: Use convexity of phi(.,y) and the x-subgradient gx(xt,yt) to upper bound the primal side.
Use concavity of phi(x,.) and the y-supergradient gy(xt,yt) to upper bound the dual side.
Add the two one-sided bounds and identify the product-space stochastic-gradient vector g(zt).
Apply the weighted-average definition of tilde z_j and convexity-concavity to move from the output gap to a weighted sum over iterates.
Substitute the single-iterate product-space gap bound into the weighted max-min expression, giving the reduction to the maximized regret-like sum.
Invoke Lemma 4.6 to bound the expectation of the maximized regret-like sum.
Substitute (4.3.9) into (4.3.8) and take expectation to obtain the displayed expected error bound.
Specialize to the paper's fixed-horizon constant stepsize.

Record the paper's printed fixed-horizon consequence after substituting the constant stepsize (4.3.15) into the general expected bound. The source prints this without an expectation, so the expectation-drop or notation change is intentionally left as a source-level unresolved passage rather than supplied as an added hypothesis.

Record (4.3.16) as the paper's printed componentwise fixed-horizon consequence. The display includes alpha_x and alpha_y, which are not defined in the cited local source window, so this step does not claim derivation from (4.3.5) alone.

Record the paper's first saddle-specific adaptation from the minimization discussion in Section 3.2: pass from fixed-horizon constant stepsizes to the printed decreasing policy. The Section 3.2 exercise proof is not printed here, so it is not used as a formal proof dependency.
Record the paper's second saddle-specific adaptation: replace averaging over all iterates by the printed sliding average over the final half-window.

Record (4.3.17) only as the source's printed saddle consequence of the decreasing-stepsize and sliding-averaging passage. The PDF says this is obtained as in the minimization case but does not print the Section 3.2 derivation in this window.
Define the diameter quantity that appears in the saddle efficiency estimate.

key_lemmas.name: Prox_mapping_Lemma_3_4
key_lemmas.statement_math: \text{Let }x_{t+1}\text{ be defined in }(3.2.5).\ \text{For any }y\in X,\ \text{we have}\quad \gamma_t\langle g(x_t),x_{t+1}-x\rangle+V(x_t,x_{t+1})\le V(x_t,x)-V(x_{t+1},x).
key_lemmas.role: Provides the one-step optimality inequality for mirror descent prox updates; Lemma 4.3 uses it as its first step.

proof.description: Apply the optimality condition of the prox subproblem (3.2.5).
Use the prox-function identity printed as (3.2.6).
Combine the optimality condition and the prox identity to conclude Lemma 3.4; the proof line is prose-only and refers back to the lemma statement display.

key_lemmas.name: Prox_sequence_Lemma_4_3
key_lemmas.statement_math: \text{Let }\zeta_1,\ldots,\zeta_j\text{ be a sequence of elements of }\mathbb{R}^n.\ \text{Define }v_t,\ t=1,2,\ldots\text{ in }X^o\text{ as follows: }v_1\in X^o\text{ and }v_{t+1}=\arg\min_{x\in X}\{\langle\zeta_t,x\rangle+V(v_t,x)\}.\ \text{Then for any }x\in X\text{ the following inequalities hold}\quad \langle\zeta_t,v_t-x\rangle\le V(v_t,x)-V(v_{t+1},x)+\frac{1}{2}\|\zeta_t\|_*^2,\quad \sum_{t=1}^j\langle\zeta_t,v_t-x\rangle\le V(v_1,x)+\frac{1}{2}\sum_{t=1}^j\|\zeta_t\|_*^2.
key_lemmas.role: Supplies the prox recursion (4.1.41) and its summed form (4.1.42), both used in Lemma 4.6.

proof.description: Apply Lemma 3.4 to the auxiliary prox sequence vt+1 = argmin{<zeta_t,x> + V(vt,x)}.
Use strong convexity of the prox function and Cauchy-Schwarz/Young to bound the movement term.
Add the auxiliary prox three-point bound and the movement term bound to obtain the one-step inequality.
Sum (4.1.41) from t=1 to j and drop the nonnegative terminal prox term.

key_lemmas.name: Lemma_4_6_gap_sum_bound
key_lemmas.statement_math: \text{For any }j\ge 1\text{ the following inequality holds}\quad \mathbb{E}\left[\max_{z\in Z}\sum_{t=1}^j\gamma_t g(z_t)^T(z_t-z)\right]\le 2+\frac{5}{2}M^2\sum_{t=1}^j\gamma_t^2.
key_lemmas.role: This is the central estimate substituted into (4.3.8) to obtain the expected saddle-point gap bound.

proof.description: Before the displayed inequality (4.3.10), the paper says it uses (4.1.41) with \zeta_t=\gamma_tG(z_t,\xi_t). This requires the proof-side prox recursion z_{t+1}=argmin_z{<\gamma_tG(z_t,\xi_t),z>+V(z_t,z)}; this is a derived interpretation of the printed algorithm line (4.3.6), whose displayed formula is retained separately.
Use (4.1.41) with zeta_t = gamma_t G(zt,xi_t) to get the stochastic one-step prox inequality.
Introduce the oracle noise residual used throughout the proof.
Rewrite (4.3.10) in terms of g(z_t), moving the residual contribution to the right-hand side.
Sum the one-step inequality from t=1 to j, telescoping the prox terms as printed.
Introduce the auxiliary prox sequence used for the Delta_t residual: the paper applies Lemma 4.3 with v1=z1 and zeta_t=-gamma_t Delta_t.
Apply Lemma 4.3 to the auxiliary sequence from the preceding step to obtain (4.3.12).
Bound the second moment of Delta_t by the stochastic-oracle moment bound M.
proof.produces: delta_second_moment_bound: conditional unbiasedness identifies g(z_t)=E[G(z_t,xi_t)|xi_[t-1]], and the product-space moment bound applies at the random iterate z_t

proof.description: Take expectation of (4.3.12), use V(z1,.) bounded by 1 on Z, and substitute the Delta_t moment bound.
Sum (4.3.11) from t=1 to j again, this time dropping the nonpositive terminal prox term V(z_{t+1},u).
Split the residual term around the auxiliary sequence v_t, producing the martingale-centered term and the auxiliary supremum term used later.
Because zt and vt are deterministic functions of xi_[t-1] and the conditional expectation of Delta_t vanishes, the martingale cross term has zero expectation.

Take suprema over u in Z and expectations on both sides of (4.3.14), dropping the zero-expectation cross term. The residual term is printed without an expectation in this display; the expected residual supremum needed for the next line is recorded in produces as the derived object matched to (4.3.13).
Use the expected residual-supremum bound printed as (4.3.13) for the derived residual object from the preceding display.
Apply (4.3.13), use sup_u V(z1,u) <= 1, and use the M-bound on G to obtain the first printed inequality in the final chain.
Simplify the constants in the final displayed chain.
The final arithmetic chain arrives at (4.3.9); line 8460 is prose-only and the displayed formula is the Lemma 4.6 statement.

key_lemmas.name: Proposition_4_10_large_deviation_bound
key_lemmas.statement_math: \text{Suppose that conditions of the bound }(4.3.16)\text{ are verified and, further, it holds for all }(u,v)\in Z\text{ that}\quad \mathbb{E}\left[\exp\left\{\|G_x(u,v,\xi)\|_{*,X}^2/M_X^2\right\}\right]\le\exp\{1\},\quad \mathbb{E}\left[\exp\left\{\|G_y(x,y,\xi)\|_{*,Y}^2/M_Y^2\right\}\right]\le\exp\{1\}.\quad \text{Then for the stepsizes }(4.3.15)\text{ one has for any }\lambda\ge1\text{ that }\operatorname{Prob}\left\{\varepsilon_\phi(\tilde z_N)>\frac{(8+2\lambda)\sqrt{5}M}{\sqrt{N}}\right\}\le2\exp\{-\lambda\}.
key_lemmas.role: Records the paper's high-probability companion to the expected saddle-point gap bound.
